analytic.title: LAG-based Analysis for Preemptive Global Scheduling with Dynamic Cache Allocation

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In recent years, the maturation of modern multicore processor technology and its increasing adoption in critical industrial domains have posed significant challenges for real-time systems, primarily due to contention for shared cache resources and the resulting uncertainty. To address this issue, contemporary processors employ cache partitioning techniques, enhancing temporal predictability by isolating cache access among processor cores. However, this isolation technique may lead to real-time tasks missing their deadlines due to an insufficient number of cache partitions. Consequently, this paper investigates the schedulability of preemptive global Earliest Deadline First (EDF) real-time scheduling algorithms that support dynamic cache allocation. We propose an innovative LAG-based schedulability analysis method for these algorithms and present a utilization-based schedulability condition that reduces analysis time complexity while improving analysis accuracy. Lastly, the performance and efficiency of the proposed schedulability determination method are validated through simulation experiments with randomly generated tasks.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In the realm of real-time embedded systems, the application of modern multicore processors has become increasingly widespread. These multicore processors typically employ a shared last-level cache to enhance cache hit rates and expedite memory access. Although shared cache contributes to superior average performance and efficiency, it poses substantial challenges to ensuring real-time and predictable system behavior. As individual processor cores can simultaneously access shared memory, cache contention may occur when memory accessed by different cores maps to the same cache line. Consequently, tasks in the cache may be evicted by tasks executing on other cores, resulting in cache misses and significant delays. Considering concurrent tasks' cache behavior (hits or misses) under inter-core cache contention scenarios yields complex interdependencies, making it difficult to accurately predict the occurrence, frequency, and duration of delays [1]. Disregarding the impact of cache contention undermines the system's temporal determinism and predictability, which, for domains with stringent real-time requirements, may lead to catastrophic consequences.

Cache partitioning is a widely employed technique to effectively mitigate cache contention in multicore processors, such as page coloring [2], LbM [3], and CAT [4]. This approach divides shared cache into multiple cache partitions and maps processor cores to different partitions. As a result, tasks executing in parallel on distinct cores cannot evict each other's cache contents, thereby avoiding cache contention for tasks running concurrently on multicore processors. This reduces interference-induced overhead while enhancing system behavior determinism. Most existing research adopts static cache partitioning strategies, allocating cache partitions and tasks to specific processor cores offline and maintaining these assignments during runtime [3], [5]. While this method greatly simplifies the analysis, it may lead to severe resource underutilization, as other cores may remain idle when a single core is overloaded.

Researchers have also proposed global scheduling strategies supporting dynamic cache partition allocation. These strategies allow shared cache to be dynamically allocated to individual processor cores according to task requirements during system operation, while also permitting tasks to migrate across cores to fully utilize system resources. For such global scheduling strategies, the literature [3], [6] employs an analysis method based on "problem windows" to derive schedulability conditions. The window-based analysis method is a widely used approach in the real-time scheduling domain, dividing specific time windows based on task characteristics and analyzing the maximum workload within that window, ultimately deducing schedulability determination conditions. As the dynamic cache partition allocation policy dictates that released jobs can only be scheduled when available cache space is at least equal to the required cache of the corresponding task, task blocking due to insufficient cache may occur. This situation may lead to overly relaxed schedulability conditions derived from the window-based analysis method, introducing considerable and unnecessary pessimism [7].

The rationale behind the LAG-based analysis method involves comparing the processor time allocated to tasks by the target scheduling algorithm with that allocated by a virtual ideal scheduler, where LAG represents the difference in processor time allocation between the two. As the actual scheduling algorithm cannot allocate more processor time to tasks than the ideal scheduler, schedulability conditions can be deduced through proof by contradiction. This method has been traditionally employed to derive delay bounds for soft real-time tasks. Recent research has discovered that it also yields excellent results in analyzing schedulability conditions for hard real-time systems, particularly for real-time tasks with more complex execution conditions, such as self-suspending tasks [8], GANG tasks [9], [10], and DAG tasks [7], [11]. Upon examination, we find that the reasoning behind this analysis method can also be applied to global scheduling supporting dynamic cache partitioning.

This study investigates the schedulability problem of preemptive global EDF scheduling algorithms supporting dynamic cache allocation. In contrast to existing work, we propose a novel LAG-based analysis method and derive a utilization-based schedulability determination condition using this method. This not only reduces the time complexity of the analysis but also enhances its tightness. An extensive set of random experiments validates the effectiveness of the scheduling analysis, and comparisons with the problem windowbased analysis method reveal a significant improvement in the acceptance rate of randomly generated task sets.

div.head: II. RELATED WORKS
div.p: Cache partitioning techniques have gained significant attention in recent years for their applications in real-time systems due to their remarkable ability to reduce shared cache interference [4], [5], [12], [13]. There are primarily two ways to implement cache partitioning: software-based methods, such as page coloring [14], which exploit the virtual-to-physical page address mapping in operating systems to achieve cache partitioning; and hardware-based methods, such as cache locking [15] and CAT [4], with recent processors providing more efficient hardware support for cache partitioning [13], [16].

On the other hand, cache interference has been incorporated into recent schedulers and analysis methods [17]- [19]. Restricting the cache partitions accessible by each core increases task execution time; thus, effective allocation techniques are required to maximize schedulability. Cache partition allocation approaches can be broadly categorized into static allocation [4], [13], [20]- [22] dynamic allocation [3], [6]. Static allocation assigns cache partitions to cores, with the allocation remaining constant throughout the execution of the entire task set. This allocation method has a natural correlation with partitioned scheduling and significantly simplifies the analysis. However, if a cache-sensitive task requires all cache partitions to meet its deadline, other tasks on cores under static allocation are almost inevitably doomed to miss their deadlines.

Dynamic allocation assigns cache partitions to tasks, allowing cache partitions to be dynamically allocated to cores based on task requirements. Current works considering both global scheduling and dynamic cache allocation include [6] and [3]. Guan et al. [6] proposed a cache-aware non-preemptive fixed-priority scheduling (nFPca) method, which eliminates preemption overhead during task execution. However, the nonpreemptive nature may lead to priority inversion scenarios, reducing schedulability. In response, Xu et al. [3] proposed a cache-aware preemptive fixed-priority scheduling (gFPca) method, which was implemented on real hardware. Both methods employ a window-based analysis technique, encoding the schedulability problem as a linear programming problem by partitioning the problem window into core-busy and cachebusy intervals. In contrast, our approach, based on the LAG method, is applicable to more general scheduling strategies, improving not only schedulability but also reducing analysis time.

div.head: III. PRELIMINARY A. Task Model
div.p: We consider a multi-core processor that supports shared cache partitioning. The processor consists of M independent homogeneous cores and A equally-sized independent cache partitions. All cores can access these cache partitions.

Consider an independent sporadic task set τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n }. Task τ i is represented by a quadruple (e i , d i , p i , a i ), where e i denotes the worst-case execution time (WCET) of the task, d i denotes the relative deadline of the task, which is the time length that the task must be completed after release, p i denotes the period of the task, which is the minimum time interval between two consecutive releases of task instances, and a i denotes the number of cache partitions that the task needs to occupy. The essential difference from the traditional tasks is that the tasks in this paper occupy a fixed size cache during their execution. The number of cache partitions occupied by a single task does not exceed the total number of cache partitions in the processor, i.e., 0 ≤ a i ≤ A.

In this paper, we focus on the implicit deadline tasks, where the deadline d i of task τ i is equal to its period p i . The slack time of task τ i is S i = d ie i . The utilization of task τ i is defined as u i = ei pi . The cache utilization of task τ i is defined as u a i = a i • ei pi . The utilization of task set τ is defined as U = ∀τi∈τ u i , and the cache utilization of τ is defined as U a = ∀τi∈τ u a i . Each sporadic task τ i releases an infinite sequence of jobs, where the arrival time of each job is separated by at least p i time units. The j-th job is denoted by τ j i , and the sequence of jobs can be represented as τ 1 i , τ 2 i , ..., τ j i , .... The release time of job τ j i is denoted by r j i , the completion time of the job is denoted by f j i , the absolute deadline is denoted by d j i , and the latest start time is denoted by l j i , where d j i = r j i + d i , l j i = r j i + S i . Each job of τ i reserves a i cache partitions at most e i time units. Thus we define the cache demand of a job as an a i × e i rectangle in the time space. Similarly, the execution demand of a job is defined as e i .

div.head: B. Cache-aware Scheduling
div.p: In this section, a preemptive global EDF scheduling algorithm that supports cache partitioning (referred to as gEDFca) is presented. This algorithm applies the EDF policy to cacheaware global scheduling: jobs with earlier absolute deadlines are assigned higher priority. Unlike the classical global EDF, gEDFca always allows M ready tasks to be executed in parallel, while considering the limitation of available cache partitions.

Specifically, gEDFca always makes scheduling decisions when a job completes or is released: given sufficient cache partitions and cores, the highest-priority task (i.e., with the earliest absolute deadline) is always selected for execution (including preempting other lower-priority tasks that occupy cache partitions and cores). For any job τ j i , it can be scheduled for execution if it satisfies the following conditions:

• At least one core is available other than those occupied by higher-priority tasks. • At least A i cache partitions are available other than those occupied by higher-priority tasks. • τ j i is the highest-priority task among all tasks that satisfy the above conditions.
As this paper only considers constrained-deadline tasks, i.e., d i ≤ p i , each task can have at most one job executing at any given time. The pseudocode of the algorithm is shown below.

div.head: Algorithm 1 gEDFca algorithm
div.formula: INPUT: Ready task queue Q ready OUTPUT: Running task queue Q run 1: Q run ← ∅ 2: Q ready ← All ready tasks 3: while Q ready = ∅ do 4: τ i ← first(Q ready ) 5: if (1 + |Q run | ≤ M ) ∧ (A i + τk∈Qrun A k ≤ A) then 6: Q run ← Q run ∪ τ i 7: end if 8: Q ready ← Q ready /τ i 9: end while 10: RETURN schedule(Q run )
div.p: The input of Algorithm 1 is the ready task queue Q ready , which contains all released but unfinished tasks sorted by the earliest absolute deadline. The output of the algorithm is the execution queue Q run . The function first(Q ready ) returns the highest priority task (i.e., the task with the earliest absolute deadline) in the queue Q ready . The function schedule(Q run ) schedules the execution queue Q run by keeping the currently executing task if it is in the queue, releasing the cores and cache partitions occupied by the task if it is not in the queue (i.e., being preempted), and letting the tasks in the queue Q run but not currently executing use the remaining cores and resources to start execution.

The first line of the algorithm initializes the queues Q run and Q ready . The main process of generating the execution queue Q run is implemented in lines 3 to 9 of the algorithm. In each iteration of the loop, the task with the earliest absolute deadline in the current ready tasks is identified (line 4), and the current core and cache partition constraints are checked (line 5). If the constraints are satisfied, the task is added to the execution queue Q run (line 6), and the task is removed from the ready queue Q ready at the end of the loop (line 8). The algorithm repeats the above loop until Q ready is empty. At the end of the algorithm, the current execution queue can be obtained. Note that although the algorithm uses the earliest deadline first policy, high-priority tasks with larger cache demands may be blocked due to the limited cache space. To reduce the waste of system resources, the algorithm allows other tasks with later deadlines but satisfying the cache space constraints to use idle resources and execute first in such cases. I, a task set τ contains three independent deadline-constrained tasks. Suppose all tasks in task set τ are released at time 0. Fig. 1 presents a specific example of task set τ scheduled by the gEDFca scheduling algorithm. In Fig. 1, at time 0, τ 1 1 , τ 1 2 , and τ 1 3 are released simultaneously. Although τ 1 2 has the same priority as τ 1

(absolute deadline 4), the highest priority task τ 1 1 occupies two cache partitions, causing τ 1 2 to be blocked due to insufficient cache availability. Therefore, τ 1 3 takes advantage of the remaining cache and processor resources and executes first. At time 1, τ 1 1 completes its execution, releasing the occupied core and cache. Consequently, the blocked task τ 1 2 can now execute. Similarly, at time 2, τ 2 1 is released. Since τ 1 2 has the same absolute deadline as τ 2 1 , and τ 2 1 needs to occupy two cache partitions, τ 2 1 remains blocked even in the presence of an idle processor (core 1) until τ 1 2 completes at time 3 and releases resources.

div.head: A. LAG-based analysis technique
div.p: Before introducing the analysis technique based on LAG, it is necessary to introduce the concept of an ideal scheduling (IS), which is a theoretical and virtual scheduling strategy that does not actually exist. This kind of scheduling usually satisfies certain special properties and is generally used to assist in proving the properties of other existing scheduling strategies. The following is a description of an ideal scheduling:
div.formula: Definition 1. A task τ i is active at time t if there exists a job τ j i such that r j i ≤ t < d j i .
div.p: Definition 2 (Resource sharing schedule). For any task set τ that supports dynamic cache allocation, Resource Sharing (RS) scheduling is an ideal scheduling. Under RS scheduling, a task τ i satisfies two properties: 1) task τ i occupies cache of size u a i ; 2) task τ i executes at a speed equal to its utilization u i (i.e., at any active time of task τ i , it completes u i portion of its workload).

Note that if the utilization rate U and cache utilization rate U a of a task set τ are not greater than M and A, respectively, then the task set τ has an RS schedule. Furthermore, although the cache occupied by task τ i is reduced to u a i under the RS schedule, the cache demand during the active period of the task remains the same, i.e., u a i • d i = a i • d i . Fig. 2 presents an example of an RS schedule. I, a task set τ consists of three mutually independent implicit-deadline tasks. Assuming that all tasks in the task set τ are released at time 0, Fig. 2 shows an example of the task set τ under an RS schedule. Since the execution speed of a task is equal to its utilization, the execution time of a task under an RS schedule is equal to its period. Furthermore, under an RS schedule, the cache occupied by a task at each time during its execution period is equal to its cache utilization rate. Therefore, under the RS schedule, task τ 1 has an execution time of 2, occupies 0.5 processor core and 1 cache partition during its execution period; task τ 2 has an execution time of 4, occupies 0.5 processor core and 1 cache partition during its execution period; task τ 3 has an execution time of 4, occupies 0.5 processor core and 0.5 cache partition during its execution period. Note that although the processor cores and cache partitions occupied by the tasks have changed under the RS schedule, the task execution and cache demand remain unchanged.

The approach based on LAG analysis involves comparing the execution time allocation and cache allocation of an arbitrary schedule (referred to as S) with that of the corresponding RS schedule, and quantifying the difference between the two to derive the schedulability condition. First, we analyze the time allocation and cache allocation at the task level: Let A(τ j i , t 1 , t 2 , S) denote the time allocation of job τ j i in the time interval [t 1 , t 2 ) under the S schedule; correspondingly, A a (τ j i , t 1 , t 2 , S) represents the cache allocation of job τ j i in the time interval [t 1 , t 2 ) under the S schedule. Thus, under the S schedule, the time allocation of task τ i in the time interval [t 1 , t 2 ) is given by:
div.formula: A(τ i , t 1 , t 2 , S) = j≥1 A(τ j i , t 1 , t 2 , S)
div.p: Correspondingly, under the S schedule, the cache allocation of task τ i in the time interval [t 1 , t 2 ) is given by:
div.formula: A a (τ i , t 1 , t 2 , S) = j≥1 A a (τ j i , t 1 , t 2 , S)
div.p: Considering that the cache size occupied by job τ j i during execution is denoted by a i , it follows that:
div.formula: a i × A(τ j i , t 1 , t 2 , S) = A a (τ j i , t 1 , t 2 , S)(1)
div.p: Let RS denote the RS schedule corresponding to the schedule S, where the time allocation and cache allocation of all jobs in RS are consistent with those in S.

div.head: Definition 3 (Lag). The lag of job τ j
div.p: i at time t is the difference between the allocation of the RS and S schedules in the time interval [0, t], specifically: lag(τ j i , t, S) = A(τ j i , 0, t, RS) -A(τ j i , 0, t, S) Definition 4 (Cache lag). The cache lag of job τ j i at time t is the difference between the cache partition allocation of the RS and S schedules in the time interval [0, t], specifically: lag a (τ j i , t, S) = A a (τ j i , 0, t, RS) -A a (τ j i , 0, t, S) Similarly, the delay of task τ i at time t is the difference between the workloads of the RS and S schedules in the time interval [0, t], as follows:
div.formula: lag(τ i , t, S) = j≥1 lag(τ j i , t, S) = j≥1 (A(τ j i , 0, t, RS) -A(τ j i , 0, t, S)) (2)
div.p: The cache delay of task τ i at time t is the difference between the cache workloads of the RS and S schedules in the time interval [0, t], as follows:
div.formula: lag a (τ i , t, S) = j≥1 lag a (τ j i , t, S) = j≥1 (A a (τ j i , 0, t, RS) -A a (τ j i , 0, t, S))(3)
div.p: Example 3. Fig. 3 presents an example of job's lag and cache lag. Let us consider a task τ i = (2, 4, 4, 2). Assuming that under scheduling policy S, the execution of task τ i begins at time 3 due to some reason, during the time interval [0, 4), task τ i executes for 1 unit of time on processor 1. Therefore, the time allocation is A(τ i , 0, 4, S) = 1 × 1 = 1, and during this time, task τ i occupies 2 cache partitions, resulting in a cache allocation of A a (τ i , 0, 4, S) = 1 × 2 = 2. By definition, the utilization of task τ i is u i = 0.5, and the cache utilization is u a i = 1. Thus, under scheduling policy RS, the time allocation of task τ i during the time interval [0, 4) is A(τ i , 0, 4, RS) = 0.5 × 4 = 2, and the cache allocation is A a (τ i , 0, 4, RS) = 1×4 = 4. Consequently, according to the definition, the lag of task τ i during the time interval [0, 4) is lag(τ i , 4, S) = 2-1 = 1, and the cache lag is lag a (τ i , 4, S) = 4 -2 = 2.
div.formula: LAG a (τ, t, S) = τi∈τ lag a (τ i , t, S)(5)
div.p: Suppose that under scheduling policy S, task set τ is unschedulable. Let t d represent the time at which the first deadline is missed in this schedule, and let job τ q p represent the first job that misses the deadline d q p at time t d . Since this section is concerned with preemptive earliest deadline first (EDF) scheduling, for all jobs with absolute deadlines later than t d , their priority is lower than that of τ q p , and therefore, they do not affect the scheduling of jobs with deadlines earlier than t d . Hence, for simplicity, in the following text, we remove all jobs with absolute deadlines later than t d from τ . Theorem 1. If there exists a job τ q p that misses its deadline at time t d under scheduling policy S, then we have LAG(τ, t d , S) > 0 and LAG a (τ, t d , S) > 0.

Proof. In the schedule S, for any task τ i that has not missed its deadline by time t d , the completed workload and cache load are equal to those in the RS schedule since the deadline has not been missed. According to the definition of lag, lag(τ i , t d , S) = 0 and lag a (τ i , t d , S) = 0 hold.

As the job τ q p under the S schedule misses its deadline at time t d , this is equivalent to the job τ q p not completing the amount of work it should have completed in the time interval [0, t d ] under the S schedule. Therefore, A(τ q p , 0, t d , RS) > A(τ q p , 0, t d , S) holds. Similarly, A a (τ q p , 0, t d , RS) > A a (τ q p , 0, t d , S). Using Eq. ( 2) and Eq. ( 3), if any task τ p has a job that misses its deadline at time t d , then lag(τ p , t d , S) > 0 and lag a (τ p , t d , S) > 0 hold simultaneously.
According to Definition 5, if there is a job in the task set τ that misses its deadline at time t d , then LAG(τ, t d , S) > 0 and LAG a (τ, t d , S) > 0 hold simultaneously.

div.head: B. Utilization-based scheduliability test
div.p: Definition 6 (Execution interval). A time interval [t 1 , t 2 ) where t 1 < t 2 , is said to be an execution interval for τ i if there exists one job of τ i that is executing throughout the interval, i.e., 1) one core and 2) a i cache partitions are used for executing one job of τ i in the interval; otherwise, it is said to be a non-execution interval for τ i . Definition 7. A time interval [t 1 , t 2 ) where t 1 < t 2 , is said to be busy for τ if all M cores are executing tasks of τ throughout the interval, i.e. no core is idle over the interval; otherwise, it is said to be non-busy for τ . Definition 8 (Non-execution core-busy/cache-busy interval).

div.head: For a non-execution interval [t 1 , t 2 ) of task τ i , if the processor is busy at any time during this interval (i.e., there is no idle processor), then this interval is called the non-execution corebusy interval of task τ i . If at any time during this interval, all processor cores are non-busy (i.e., at least one processor core is idle), then this interval is called the non-execution cachebusy interval of task τ i .
div.p: By applying the analysis technique of execution-busy interval partitioning, we can easily deduce that if a job τ j i is released during its non-execution interval but remains unfinished, it can be attributed to one of two possibilities: either all processor cores are busy, or there are at most A i -1 free cache partitions available. These possibilities correspond to the non-execution core-busy interval and non-execution cachebusy interval, respectively. Definition 9 (Earliest positive LAG time instant). If the task set τ misses its deadline for the first time at time t d under gEDFca scheduling, then the earliest positive LAG time t 0 of τ (0 < t 0 ≤ t d ) is the earliest instant within the time interval [0, t d ) that satisfies:
div.formula: LAG(τ, t 0 , gDEF ca) > 0(6)
div.p: Based on Theorem 1 and LAG(τ, 0, gEDF ca) = 0, the earliest positive LAG time instant t 0 is well defined. Furthermore, according to Theorem 1 and LAG a (τ, 0, gEDF ca) = 0, the task also needs to occupy the corresponding cache during execution, and time t 0 also satisfies: LAG a (τ, t 0 , gEDF ca) > 0 (7)

Corollary 1. If task set τ misses a deadline under gED-Fca scheduling, then there exists at least one task, denoted as τ l , that satisfies lag(τ l , t 0 , gEDF ca) > 0 and lag a (τ l , t 0 , gEDF ca) > 0.

Proof. According to the definition, LAG of task set τ at time t 0 is equal to the sum of lag of all tasks at time t 0 . Thus, according to Eq.( 6), there is at least one task in τ with lag greater than 0 at time t 0 . Let τ l denote such a task, we have: lag(τ l , t 0 , gEDF ca) > 0. According to Eq.( 1) and ( 3), we have for task τ l : lag a (τ l , t 0 , gEDF ca) = a l × lag(τ l , t 0 , gEDF ca) > 0.

Since the lag of task τ l at t 0 is greater than 0, τ l has at least one job released before time t 0 that was not finished at time t 0 . Since t d is the earliest time instant when a job misses its deadline, we have t 0 ≤ t d . Moreover, since there are no multiple jobs of any deadline task in a single period, task τ l has only one job released before t 0 and not finished at time t 0 . Let τ h l denote this job, and let r h l denote the release time of job τ h l . Since there are no other jobs that miss their deadlines before time t d , and r h l < t 0 ≤ t d , all jobs released before time r h l of task τ l have been finished under gEDFca scheduling. Similarly, under RS scheduling, all jobs released before time r h l of task τ l have been finished. Therefore, lag(τ l , r h l , gEDF ca) = 0 at time r h l for task τ l . Similarly, lag a (τ l , r h l , gEDF ca) = 0. Let E denote the cumulative time during which the job τ h l is executed in the time interval [r h l , t 0 ), i.e., the length of execution intervals within [r h l , t 0 ). Let Ē signify the cumulative time during which the job τ h l is not executed and no processor cores are idle in the time interval [r h l , t 0 ), i.e., the length of non-execution, core-busy intervals within [r h l , t 0 ). Let Ēa represent the cumulative time during which the job τ h l is not executed and at least one processor core is idle in the time interval [r h l , t 0 ), i.e., the length of non-execution, cache-busy intervals within [r h l , t 0 ). As illustrated in Figure 4, according to the aforementioned definitions, it holds that:
div.formula: t 0 -r h l = E + Ē + Ēa (8)
div.p: Lemma 1. If the task set τ experiences a missed deadline under gEDFca scheduling, there exists a task τ l such that lag(τ l , t 0 , gEDF ca) > 0, and this task satisfies:
div.formula: U > min A -a l + 1 max τi∈τ a i , M -1 (1 -u l ) + u l (9)
div.p: Proof. According to Corollary 1, given the unschedulability of the task set τ under gEDFca scheduling, there exists a task τ l such that lag(τ l , t 0 , gEDF ca) > 0. Leveraging the properties of lag, the lag of task τ l at time t 0 can be calculated as follows: lag(τ l , t 0 , gEDF ca) =lag(τ l , r h l , gEDF ca) + A(τ l , r h l , t 0 , RS) -A(τ l , r h l , t 0 , gEDF ca) Because lag(τ l , r h l , gEDF ca) = 0, according to Corollary 1, we have:
div.formula: lag(τ l , t 0 , gEDF ca) =A(τ l , r h l , t 0 , RS) -A(τ l , r h l , t 0 , gEDF ca) > 0(10)
div.p: Since job τ h l is released at time r h l and is not completed at time t 0 , based on the definition of execution interval in Def. 6, it is known that under gEDFca scheduling, job τ h l is executed on a processor core at every point in time during the E interval. According to the definition of RS scheduling, the execution rate of job τ h l under RS scheduling is equal to its utilization u l . Based on Eq. ( 8), we have:
div.formula: A(τ l , r h l , t 0 , RS) -A(τ l , r h l , t 0 , gEDF ca) ≤(E + Ē + Ēa ) × u l -E × 1(11)
div.p: Furthermore, we know u l = el pl ≤ 1. Note that if u l = 1, then U > A-al+1 maxτ i ∈τ ai (1u l ) + u l = u l holds, as n > 1 and e k > 0 for all k. Consequently, considering the case where u l < 1, we obtain:

div.formula: (E + Ē + Ēa ) × u l -E > 0. Thus ( Ē + Ēa )u l > E -E × u l > 0, as 0 < u l < 1, we have: Ē + Ēa > 0
div.p: According to Eq. ( 6), LAG(τ, t 0 , gEDF ca) > 0 and LAG(τ, r h l , gEDF ca) ≤ 0, thus LAG(τ, t 0 , gEDF ca) -LAG(τ, r h l , gEDF ca) > 0. Based on the definition, we have:
div.formula: LAG(τ, t 0 , gEDF ca) -LAG(τ, r h l , gEDF ca) =LAG(τ, r h l , gEDF ca) + A(τ, r h l , t 0 , RS) -A(τ, r h l , t 0 , gEDF ca) -LAG(τ, r h l , gEDF ca) =A(τ, r h l , t 0 , RS) -A(τ, r h l , t 0 , gEDF ca) > 0(13)
div.p: According to the definition of non-execution intervals in Def. 8, it is evident that under the gEDFca scheduling: at every instant during Ē, all M processor cores are busy; moreover, at every instant during Ēa , at least one processor core is idle. As job τ h l cannot execute during Ēa despite the availability of idle processors, at least Aa l + 1 cache partitions are occupied by other tasks. A single task in task set τ occupies at most max τi∈τ a i cache partitions, thus during Ēa , at least min A-al+1 maxτ i ∈τ ai , M -1 other tasks are executing. Let B = min A-al+1 maxτ i ∈τ ai , M -1 . Since each core can execute only one task at any given time, during Ēa , at least B processor cores are busy. Through the aforementioned analysis, we can derive:

V. EVALUATION

div.head: A. Experimental Setup
div.p: In this section, we employ a randomly generated set of implicit-deadline tasks, with parameter settings consistent with those presented in [6]. Specifically, the number of processor cores, denoted as M , is set to 6, and the number of cache partitions, denoted as A, is set to 40. Task periods are uniformly distributed within the range [10,20], with deadlines equal to their respective periods. Worst-case execution times are determined by the product of the task's utilization and its period. In Figure 5, the task utilization u i and the number of cache partitions a i are categorized into three classes based on task type, following the parameters in [6]: in Fig. 5a,u i is uniformly distributed within [0.1, 0.3], while a i is uniformly distributed within [1,5]; in Fig. 5b, u i is uniformly distributed within [0.1, 0.6], while a i is uniformly distributed within [1,5]; in Fig. 5c, u i is uniformly distributed within [0.1, 0.3], while a i is uniformly distributed within [2,10]. Similarly, tasks in Figure 6 are also divided into three types: in Fig. 6a, u i is uniformly distributed within [0.1, 0.3], while a i is uniformly distributed within [5,20]; in Fig. 6b, u i is uniformly distributed within [0.1, 0.6], while a i is uniformly distributed within [5,20]; in Fig. 6c, u i is uniformly distributed within [0.1, 0.3], while a i is uniformly distributed within [20,35].

Task sets are generated iteratively, with each iteration pro-ducing one random task that satisfies the parameter settings and adding it to the task set until the sum of the task set's utilization (cache utilization, respectively) exceeds the target value. Subsequently, the utilization (cache utilization, respectively) of the last task is reduced to make the sum of the utilizations (cache utilizations, respectively) of all tasks in the set equal to the target value. We tested 1000 random generated task sets for each point on the curve. The experiments are conducted on a Laptop PC equipped with an AMD Ryzen 7 5800H processor (3.2GHz) and 16GB of main memory. We use open source tools Python-MIP [23] as LP solver to solve the LP formulation in the experiments.

div.head: B. Experimental results
div.p: We compare the schedulability of different methods, where gEDFca is our LAG-based approach; while gFPca [3], nFPca-T1 and nFPca-T2 [6] are window-based approach. Fig. 6 and Fig. 5 show the fraction of schedulable task sets under the corresponding methods when changing U and U a , respectively. From the experimental results, we observe that the LAGbased method demonstrates superior performance compared to the window-based methods in nearly all cases. Particularly when the task utilization u i and required cache a i are low, as shown in Fig. 5a, the LAG-based method exhibits a commendable performance. This is attributed to the higher values of 1-u i and A-a i +1 in Eq. ( 18) when u i and a i are low, which evidently contributes to enhanced schedulability. However, when the task utilization u i is high, as depicted in Fig. 5b, the performance of the LAG-based method experiences a significant decline. This occurs because when u i is high, 1-u i becomes smaller, as illustrated in Eq. ( 18) , which has a considerably negative impact on the schedulability of the task set. Additionally, we observe an unintuitive increase in the performance of the LAG-based method when the distribution range of a i rises above A/2, as higher values of min(a i ) and max(a i ) in Eq. ( 18) facilitate improved schedulability.

Table II presents the analysis time required for different methods. Experimental results indicate that when processing task sets containing 1100 tasks on our experimental platform, the LAG-based schedulability analysis method requires less than 0.5 seconds, while the LP-based analysis methods, nFPca-T1 and gFPca, demand more than 6800 seconds and 2900 seconds, respectively. This is due to the substantial simplification of the analysis process achieved by the utilization-based schedulability condition. Moreover, nFPca-T2, as an overapproximation of nFPca-T1, requires a significantly shorter time (less than 0.8 seconds) due to its lower time complexity. Therefore, compared to LP-based analysis methods, the LAG-based schedulability analysis method exhibits higher efficiency.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: Shared cache partitioning techniques offer a means to reduce the uncertainty in task execution times. This paper presents a global EDF scheduling algorithm that supports dynamic cache allocation and proposes a LAG-based schedulability analysis method for this algorithm. Through this method, a utilization-based schedulability condition is derived, which not only reduces the computational complexity of schedulability analysis but also yields more accurate analysis results. Finally, random experiments demonstrate that the proposed analysis method exhibits high efficiency and performance.
